reconstruction.statement:
Let C be a connected compact Riemann surface, x∈C, and (L,h) a smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle with semipositive curvature strictly positive on C\{x}. Fix an integer r≥1. In a coordinate z centered at x and a holomorphic frame, suppose |e|_h^2=e^{−φ} and φ(z)=|z|^{2r}+O(|z|^{2r+1}). Let ν be a smooth positive volume form, locally a(z)dA with a(0)=1. For integers q=q_m→∞ with q=o(m), let V_m=H^0(C,L^m⊗m_x^q), normed by ∫_C|s|_{h^m}^2dν, and let B_m be its Bergman density, with value zero if V_m=0. Put ρ=φ_{z\bar z}, t=q/m, R=(q/(mr))^{1/(2r)}, and Φ(u)=(2π)^{−1/2}∫_{−∞}^u e^{−s^2/2}ds. Let the actual obstacle boundary be
Γ_t={R c_R(θ)e^{iθ}},
where c_R=1+O(R) is the boundary function supplied by the supporting geometric result.

1. Optimal universal uncorrected range and exact fixed-weight criterion.
For every integer r≥1, the optimal universal range for the law in the question is
q_m→∞, q_m=o(m^{1/(r+1)}).
In this range, for every permissible metric and volume form, every fixed real τ and every sequence of observation points satisfying
m|z(x_m)|^{2r}=q_m/r+τ√(q_m/r),
one has
πB_m(x_m)/(mr^2|z(x_m)|^{2r−2})→Φ(τ).
The convergence is uniform in observation direction and for τ in compact real intervals. For every sublinear growth sequence outside this range and every r≥1, there is a compact example satisfying the original hypotheses for which the asserted limit fails. For a fixed permissible weight and a fixed sequence q_m, the assertion for every observation direction and every fixed τ holds if and only if
√q ||c_R−1||_∞→0.
The observation radii satisfy
|z|/R=1+τ/(2√(rq))+O(q^{−1}),
and
√qR=r^{−1/(2r)}q^{(r+1)/(2r)}m^{−1/(2r)}.

2. Complete smooth-weight correction throughout all sublinear growth.
Let D_t be the obstacle hole bounded by Γ_t, let d_t(z) be signed Euclidean distance to Γ_t, positive outside, and let p_t(z) be its nearest boundary point. The hole satisfies
∫_{D_t}ρ(z)f(z)dA=πt f(0)
for every f holomorphic near its closure. The leading density is mρ(z)/(πa(z)), and the normal transition length is
ℓ(p)=1/(2√(mρ(p))).
For every sequence with d_t(z)=o(R),
πa(z)B_m(z)/(mρ(z))−Φ(d_t(z)/ℓ(p_t(z)))→0.
This holds uniformly in angle on bounded corrected Gaussian bands. When d_t=o(R) but d_t/ℓ→−∞ or +∞, the normalized density tends respectively to 0 or 1. Thus Γ_t is the corrected center for arbitrary original smooth weights and every q→∞, q=o(m); it need not be circular. Further weight terms can move this center by arbitrarily many transition widths. Uniformly on the boundary,
ρ(p)=r^2R^{2r−2}(1+O(R)),
so the relative correction to the leading normal scale tends to zero. The smooth volume enters the leading density through 1/a and does not change this limiting center or scale.

3. First critical Taylor correction.
Write
φ(z)=|z|^{2r}+P_{2r+1}(z,\bar z)+O(|z|^{2r+2}),
where P_{2r+1} is the real homogeneous Taylor polynomial of degree 2r+1, and let P(θ)=P_{2r+1}(e^{iθ},e^{−iθ}). Define the circle Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator by Λ(e^{inθ})=|n|e^{inθ}. Then
c_R(θ)=1+Rb_1(θ)+O(R^2),
b_1(θ)=−[((2r+1)−Λ)P](θ)/(4r^2).
In particular the harmonic modes of frequencies ±(2r+1) do not affect the center.
If q=O(m^{1/(r+1)}), then √qR is bounded and √qR^2→0. At the original observation points, with θ=arg z, the corrected Gaussian argument is
τ−2√(rq)Rb_1(θ)+o(1)
=τ+[√qR/(2r^{3/2})][((2r+1)−Λ)P](θ)+o(1).
Consequently,
πB_m(z)/(mr^2|z|^{2r−2})
−Φ(τ+[√qR/(2r^{3/2})][((2r+1)−Λ)P](θ))→0,

in every fixed required finite boundary norm, for sufficiently small R. Each b_j depends only on the Taylor jet of φ through degree 2r+j. The coefficients are invariant under addition of harmonic terms to φ; in general they include nonlinear contributions from lower nonharmonic terms.

has physical center error O(R^{J+2}). Replacing the actual boundary by this curve in the signed-normal-distance correction is valid whenever
√qR^{J+1}→0,

For f(u)=u^r, the center equation is mrR^{2r}=q and σ^2(R^2)=rq. If
f(u)=u^r+c u^{r+1}+⋯,
then
m[r u_*^r+c(r+1)u_*^{r+1}+⋯]=q,
σ^2(u)=m[r^2u^r+c(r+1)^2u^{r+1}+⋯].

If q is of order m/log m, then R is of order (log m)^{−1/(2r)} and

With dd^c=(i/(2π))∂\bar∂ and Euclidean area dA,
dd^cφ=(ρ/π)dA,
dd^c(2t log|z|)=tδ_x,
ρ(z)=r^2|z|^{2r−2}(1+O(|z|)),
∫_{|z|<R}r^2|z|^{2r−2}dA=πrR^{2r}.

reconstruction.proof:
We import the obstacle theorem w103-1/n1 and the complete kernel theorem w103-1/n3, as allowed by the declared support. Write q=q_m, R=(q/(mr))^(1/(2r)), and c=c_R. All limiting statements below are uniform in angle when their arguments stay bounded; for unbounded arguments we use the saturation part of the imported kernel theorem.

1. Raw observations and the exact criterion. Expansion of the specified observation radius gives, uniformly for bounded τ,
 |z|/R=(1+τ√(r/q))^(1/(2r))
       =1+τ/(2√(rq))+O(q^(-1)).                    (10)
The C^2 norm of c-1 is O(R). In a tubular neighborhood the signed distance of a point on a fixed radial ray to the graph R c(θ)e^(iθ) has the same sign as |z|-Rc(θ), and equals this radial difference times 1+o(1), uniformly when the difference is o(R). This follows either from the normal projection equations or by Taylor expanding the graph; its normal makes angle O(R) with the radial direction. If the radial difference is O(R/√q), its scaled-distance error is o(1). The imported edge scale is 2√(rq)/R times signed distance, to relative error O(R).

Consequently √q||c-1||_∞→0 implies that the corrected argument at (10) is τ+o(1), proving the raw law. Conversely, if this norm does not tend to zero, choose an angle maximizing |c-1| and take τ=0. Along a subsequence the scaled displacement has a fixed sign and magnitude bounded away from zero; pass further to a finite nonzero magnitude limit or to infinity. The corrected argument then has a nonzero limit or tends to signed infinity. The imported law or saturation contradicts the required value Φ(0)=1/2. This proves the exact fixed-weight all-direction criterion. In converting normalizations we used
 a(z)→1,   ρ(z)/(r²|z|^(2r-2))→1
uniformly on the shrinking annulus.

Since c-1=O(R), a universal sufficient condition is √qR→0. The identity
 √qR=r^(-1/(2r))q^((r+1)/(2r))m^(-1/(2r))
makes this exactly q=o(m^(1/(r+1))). The sharp examples in paragraph 6 below prove necessity for universality, including for oscillatory growth sequences. This also proves the asserted compact-τ uniformity.

2. Exact correction. The imported obstacle gives the center Γ_t, its holomorphic moment identity, and its curvature mass t=q/m. The imported kernel theorem gives, for every d_t=o(R),
 πa(z)B_m(z)/(mρ(z))=Φ(2√(mρ(p_t(z)))d_t(z))+o(1),
with both saturations. This is the claimed complete smooth-weight theorem. Its boundary curvature is ρ(p)=r²R^(2r-2)(1+O(R)), hence the stated length. This relative error tends to zero, but a displacement of the boundary of size R² already measures √qR transition widths. The volume affects the leading density, not this center or normal length.

3. Linearized boundary calculation. It is useful to do the calculation for an arbitrary first effective degree n=2r+j. Suppose the earlier nonharmonic perturbations have been removed or vanish. Put Q_R=Q_0+R^j P_n+O(R^(j+1)), and write c_R=1+R^j b+O(R^(j+1)). Linearizing the matching value equation on the moving circle gives
 2Re δG|_{S¹}=P_n|_{S¹}=:P;
the displacement terms cancel because Q_0 and U_0 have the same first normal derivative. The harmonic function with boundary value P has normal derivative ΛP. Linearizing the normal-derivative matching gives
 (Q_0″(1)-U_0″(1))b+nP-ΛP=0.
Since Q_0″(1)-U_0″(1)=4r², we obtain
 b=-[(n-Λ)P]/(4r²).                              (11)
For j=1 this proves the displayed b_1 formula. Harmonic homogeneous polynomials have only frequencies ±n and are killed by n-Λ. Every other mode of a homogeneous polynomial of degree n has frequency of magnitude at most n-2.

If q=O(m^(1/(r+1))), then √qR is bounded and √qR²→0. Substitution of c=1+Rb_1+O(R²) into (10) and into the normal-distance argument therefore gives
 τ-2√(rq)Rb_1(θ)+o(1)
 =τ+[√qR/(2r^(3/2))][((2r+1)-Λ)P](θ)+o(1).
All errors are uniform, and the kernel theorem proves the stated shifted law without any convergence assumption on θ. A smooth radial function on the plane is a smooth function of |z|² near zero, and hence has no odd-degree homogeneous radial Taylor term.

4. All finite effective jets. Smooth parameter dependence in each finite boundary norm supplies
 c_R=1+∑_{j=1}^J R^j b_j+O(R^(J+1)).
The rescaled weight through order R^J is determined by the Taylor polynomial of φ through degree 2r+J. Differentiating the implicit boundary equations successively shows that b_j uses precisely this jet: at each order its unknown coefficient is acted on by the same invertible derivative used in the supporting implicit-function construction, while the other terms involve already determined lower coefficients and the order-j weight coefficient. Harmonic invariance is exact by the obstacle theorem. This also explains why lower coefficients can enter nonlinearly.

The physical Hausdorff and C^1 error of the order-J graph is O(R^(J+2)). Signed-distance functions in a common small tubular neighborhood differ by that order; this follows from the normal-coordinate equations, whose Jacobians are uniformly invertible after dividing coordinates by R. Curvature and normal-scale factors change by a relative o(1). Therefore replacement in a bounded corrected band is valid if √qR^(J+1)→0. In unbounded bands it remains valid by saturation and the vanishing scaled error. Algebra makes this condition q=o(m^((J+1)/(r+J+1))).

If b_j is the first nonzero effective coefficient, then
 ||c-1||_∞=R^j(||b_j||_∞+O(R)).
Paragraph 1 thus makes the raw criterion precisely √qR^j→0, or q=o(m^(j/(r+j))). At its critical bounded range the next error is √qR^(j+1)=o(1), giving shift -2√(rq)R^j b_j. If √qR^j→∞, a fixed direction with nonzero b_j is inside for b_j>0 and outside for b_j<0 by many normal lengths; saturation gives zero or one.

For clarity about the first nonzero coefficient, there is no additional hidden raw-jet criterion. Inductively, if b_1,...,b_{j-1} vanish, remove the harmonic terms at these degrees. At the next degree the perturbation has no lower nonharmonic terms and its coefficient is (11). If that coefficient also vanishes, all its frequencies satisfy |n|=degree, so that term is harmonic as well. This induction proves the statement about earlier terms and the first coefficient formula. It also shows why inspecting a first raw Taylor term without removing harmonic terms is insufficient.

5. Radial case. Let φ=f(u), u=|z|². Direct differentiation gives ρ=f′+uf″ and F(u):=uf′(u) has derivative ρ(u)>0 for u>0 sufficiently small. The curvature mass of a disk of squared radius u is F(u), because
 (1/π)∫_{|z|²<u}ρ dA=∫_0^u ρ(v)dv=uf′(u).
Thus the matching hole is the disk F(u_*)=q/m. Alternatively its inner matching potential is t log u plus a constant; value and derivative matching give exactly the same equation. Uniqueness in the imported obstacle theorem identifies this disk with the actual hole.

Let A(u)=[mF(u)-q]/√(muρ(u)). For bounded normal scaled distance, Taylor's formula at u_* gives
 A(u)=2√(mρ(u_*))(√u-√u_*)+o(1).
Indeed F′=ρ, u-u_*=2√u_*(√u-√u_*)+O((√u-√u_*)²), and the denominator is √(mu_*ρ(u_*))(1+o(1)). The same calculation has a relative 1+o(1) error whenever √u-√u_*=o(R), so it preserves both signed infinite limits. The complete corrected radial law therefore follows from paragraph 2. At points staying a fixed relative distance from this shrinking center, the usual Gaussian localization outside, and the Hardy/gap estimate inside from the supporting kernel proof, give the corresponding saturation as well.

The radial monomial integral is, after v=log u,
 π∫ exp[(k+1)v-mf(e^v)] a(e^v)dv
when the volume is radial (its smooth factor does not alter the leading Hessian). The exponential's second derivative at u is -mu[f′(u)+uf″(u)]=-muρ(u). This is the leading saddle or mode variance σ²(u), not an exact variance identity. Its saddle centers on k+1=mF(u); the one-unit offset is negligible on the diverging √q scale. For f=u^r, F=r u^r, σ²=mr²u^r, so at R² the latter is rq. For f=u^r+c u^(r+1)+⋯, differentiation yields the two displayed center and variance expansions. At the raw radius R² the first numerator correction is c(r+1)mR^(2r+2), whose division by √(rq) is c(r+1)r^(-3/2)√qR². Since √qR² is order one at q of order m^(2/(r+2)), this is the first radial critical range when c≠0.

6. Compact sharp examples. Choose a sufficiently large integer d and a smooth function F on [0,∞) which equals r u^r near zero, has F′>0 for u>0, and equals d-ε/u for large u. Such a function is obtained by joining the two increasing pieces with a smooth positive derivative and choosing its integral to give the desired endpoint difference; taking d large leaves room for the joining interval. Define f′=F/u and choose the constant so f=u^r near zero. This gives a smooth potential at zero. At infinity integration gives
 f(u)=d log u+C+ε/u.
It defines a metric on O(d): in coordinate v=1/w its weight is f(|v|^(-2))+d log|v|²=C+ε|v|². Its curvature is positive at infinity and at every finite w≠0, and is r²|w|^(2r-2) near zero. Choose a positive smooth radial volume equal to dA_w near zero and smoothly positive at infinity. These choices satisfy all global hypotheses.

Now choose the local coordinate w=z+cz² with c>0 real. Its derivative at zero is one, so a_z(0)=1 and φ(z)=|z+cz²|^(2r)=|z|^(2r)+O(|z|^(2r+1)). The radial hole in w is exactly |w|<R. In z it is |z+cz²|<R, whose positive-real boundary radius is R-cR²+O(R³). At the raw τ=0 observation z=R its signed distance is cR²(1+O(R)), so the corrected argument is
 2c√r(√qR)(1+O(R)).
The requested normalization differs from the corrected one by a factor tending to one: locally ρ_z/a_z=r²|w|^(2r-2), and |w|/|z|→1. For every excluded growth sequence, √qR fails to tend to zero. A subsequence has limit κ∈(0,∞] after further selection. The supporting law gives Φ(2c√rκ) if κ<∞, and outer saturation gives one if κ=∞. Neither is 1/2. This proves sharpness for every such sequence and every r. Expansion of the coordinate change gives P(θ)=2r Re(ce^(iθ)); (11) then gives b_1=-Re(ce^(iθ)), checking the counterexample against the general coefficient formula.

7. Limits of Taylor information. For c>0 put locally
 f(u)=u^r+c u^r exp(-u^(-1/2)),
with the extra term set to zero at zero. It is smooth and flat relative to the given leading Taylor term. Differentiation shows ρ=r²u^(r-1)(1+o(1)), so curvature is positive on a sufficiently small punctured neighborhood. Extend F=uf′ monotonically as in paragraph 6 to obtain a compact example. At u=R²,
 F(u)/(r u^r)=1+c exp(-1/R)[1+1/(2rR)].
For q of order m/log m, R is of order (log m)^(-1/(2r)); hence √q exp(-1/R)/R→∞. The relative perturbation just displayed tends to zero, but is much larger than q^(-1/2). The implicit center equation, or the mean value theorem applied to F, shows that the raw circle is outside the corrected disk by an o(R) distance and by a number of widths tending to infinity. Its raw density therefore tends to one. All finite jets agree with u^r, so every finite b_j vanishes. This proves that no fixed Taylor correction can be complete throughout all sublinear growth, whereas the exact obstacle correction is complete.

8. Constants and dimension. With dA=(i/2)dz∧dz̄,
 dd^cφ=(ρ/π)dA,  dd^c(2t log|z|)=tδx.
Direct polar integration gives ∫_{|z|<R}r²|z|^(2r-2)dA=πrR^(2r). Thus the atom mass, the center mrR^(2r)=q, and the full density mρ/(πa) agree. Equation (10) gives raw argument 2√(rq)(|z|/R-1)=τ+o(1). The supporting kernel calculation gives the normal length 1/(2√(mρ)), its quadratic exponent 2η², and the half-line Gaussian with variance one. Finally the substitution v=m s^(2r) in the plane polar integral yields
 ∫_ℂ|z|^(2k)e^(-m|z|^(2r))dA=(π/r)m^(-(k+1)/r)Γ((k+1)/r).
Here the domain is ℂ, not the compact surface.

The curvature has positive integral, so the permitted degree premise gives deg L>0. The degree of L^m⊗m_x^q is m deg L-q→∞. The permitted Riemann–Roch formula implies h⁰≥m deg L-q+1-g>0 for large m. Hence the zero-space convention has no asymptotic effect. Every computation above, including the cubic angular correction, the compact construction, the flat example, and the constants, is valid without modification for r=1.

correctness.report: PASS conditional on the cited external results listed below. The regularity inference is valid: choosing arbitrarily large finite k in Forstnerič’s Hölder refinement gives arbitrarily high prescribed spatial and parameter regularity. Neither summary asserts that the cited papers themselves prove the varying-weight, fixed-residue obstacle theorem. The full text and both summaries consistently reserve the residue constraints and obstacle identification for additional arguments. In particular, a disk passing through (0,∞) need not have a prescribed Schwarz-function residue; the note correctly distinguishes these conditions.

If H¹(X,O(N))=0, nearby such curves form a manifold whose tangent space at Σ is the real fixed space H⁰_ρ(X,O(N)); the deformation result also allows sufficiently small deformations of the ambient complex manifold and totally real boundary condition. With correspondingly higher regularity, the construction works in higher Hölder spaces.

The wording also leaves unclear whether Schwarz-function existence is assumed or asserted for a prescribed φ. The source establishes the conclusions in its sole-pole setup; approving the supplied wording would require silently specifying that setup.
